title: Kitchen reads
headline: Let the dough tell you when it is ready
summary: Rising times in recipes assume a warm room. Here is how to read the dough instead.
author: Priya Nair

paragraphs.text: Most bread at home fails for one plain reason: the dough is asked to rise in a kitchen that is colder than the recipe expects. Yeast slows right down below twenty degrees, and the clock on the page keeps going anyway.

Instead of watching the clock, watch the dough. It is ready when it has grown by about half and a floured finger leaves a dent that fills back slowly. A clear container with a strip of tape at the start line helps.
Shaping matters less than people think. A loose round on a floured board, turned a few times so the top is tight, will hold well enough. Tuck the seam under and leave it alone for the second rise.

Bake hot at first and lower the heat after ten minutes. The crust sets while the inside keeps rising, which gives the open crumb most home bakers want. A tray of water on the oven floor helps the crust stay thin.

When it comes out, wait before you cut. The loaf is still cooking inside for a while, and a knife too soon turns the middle gummy. An hour on a rack is not too long, even if the kitchen smells too good to wait.
Flour changes from bag to bag too. A dough that felt right last week may need a spoon more water today, and that is normal rather than a mistake on your part.
Write down the room temperature and the time it took. After a few loaves you will know your kitchen better than any recipe does, and the clock will start to agree with the dough.
If the room is cold, an oven with only the light on is often warm enough. A bowl of hot water on the shelf below adds steam and keeps the top of the dough from drying out while it waits.
